Color memory and imagery

Instructions

Read the report and use it as a basis for your presentation. You can also download the preprocessed data from colors_and_imagery.csv and use your favorite software (JASP, jamovi, R, SPSS) to analyze it to get more insight into the study results. The data file has the following columns:

  • participant - participant identifier (factor with levels “S1”, “S2”, etc.)
  • vviq - Visual Vividness Imagery Questionnaire sum (0–64; higher scores indicate more vivid imagery)
  • afterimage_relative - second-run imagery/afterimage comparison (−2 to +2; higher means stronger imagery relative to the afterimage; unsure is missing)
  • block - block number (0 = training, 1-2 = main experimental blocks)
  • trial_number - trial number within the experiment
  • similarity_bin - angular distance between target and distractor colors in degrees (20°, 45°, or 135°)
  • target_color - the target color value in degrees (0-360°)
  • distr_color - the distractor color value in degrees (0-360°)
  • td_dist - difference between target and distractor colors in degrees
  • left_color - color value of the left stimulus in degrees
  • right_color - color value of the right stimulus in degrees
  • target_noise - noise level of the target stimulus (factor: “low” or “high”)
  • distr_noise - noise level of the distractor stimulus (factor: “low” or “high”)
  • target_x - x-coordinate of the target position (-300 for left, 300 for right)
  • distr_x - x-coordinate of the distractor position (-300 for left, 300 for right)
  • cue_n - cue number (1 = first report, 2 = second report)
  • cue_pos - position of the cue (-300 for left, 300 for right)
  • cued_color - the color value that was cued (the one to be reported) in degrees
  • resp_color - the color value reported by the participant in degrees
  • error - angular deviation between the target color and response color in degrees
  • abs_err - absolute value of the error in degrees
  • noise - combined noise condition from target and distractor (factor with 4 levels: “low - low”, “high - low”, “low - high”, “high - high”)
  • be_c - error after correction for individual biases (more reliable measure than raw error)
  • is_outlier - a boolean indicating whether the trial is an outlier to be excluded
  • abs_be_c - absolute value of the bias-corrected error
  • bias_to_distr_raw - raw bias toward the distractor in degrees
  • bias_to_distr_corr - bias-corrected bias toward the distractor in degrees

Research questions

Main theoretical question: How do stimulus noise and individual imagery ability jointly shape color memory performance?

Why is this important? Visual memory is often studied as if everyone uses the same strategy, but some studies suggest that individual differences in imagery ability can significantly impact how people approach the task. Imagine that you want to describe a color of a dress to a friend. Some people might have a very vivid mental image of the dress, while others will rely more on semantic descriptions. Understanding these differences helps connect memory mechanisms to measurable variation in experiment outcomes.

The study investigates the relationship between visual imagery ability (measured by VVIQ and an adaptation test) and color memory performance. In particular, it examines how noise in the stimulus affects memory accuracy and whether this is moderated by individual differences in imagery ability.

The empirical questions to address in your analysis include:

  1. How does noise level in the target and distractor stimuli affect color memory accuracy?
  2. How are VVIQ and adaptation-based measures of imagery related to each other?
  3. Does imagery ability predict overall color memory performance?
  4. Does imagery ability predict how strongly performance is affected by noise?
  5. Does imagery ability predict how much performance degrades when reporting the second item compared to the first?

Feel free to explore other questions as well!

Methods

Procedure

Participants first completed a browser check to ensure their screen met the minimum requirements (1000 × 600 pixels) and were instructed to switch to fullscreen mode. They then received general instructions explaining the purpose of the study and were informed that they would complete a questionnaire and an imagery task followed by a memory task. Participants completed the Visual Vividness Imagery Questionnaire and the adaptation (afterimage) task, after which they received detailed instructions for the color memory task. They then completed training on the color memory task followed by two experimental blocks with a short break halfway through each block.

Materials

The experiment was implemented using jsPsych 7.3.4, a JavaScript library for conducting behavioral experiments in a web browser.

Visual Vividness Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ)

Participants completed a shortened version of the Visual Vividness Imagery Questionnaire (Marks, 1973), which assessed their self-reported ability to form mental images. The VVIQ included four scenarios (out of the original eight): visualizing a relative or friend, a sunrise, a shop front, and a countryside scene, presented in random order. For each scenario, participants were presented with a screen containing all four specific visual details to rate simultaneously. Participants rated the vividness of each detail on a 5-point scale, from “No image at all, you only ‘know’ that you are thinking of the object” (rating = 0) to “Perfectly clear and as vivid as real seeing” (rating = 4). Higher scores indicated more vivid visual imagery.

Adaptation task

After the VVIQ, participants completed an afterimage–imagery comparison task adapted from Price et al. (2026). A high-contrast black-and-white image of a face with a red fixation dot in the centre was presented full screen on a white background for 30 s. Participants were instructed to keep their gaze on the red dot, to close their eyes as soon as the image disappeared, and to attend to any afterimage until it had completely faded, after which they clicked a button (the time until this click was recorded as the afterimage duration). Participants then reported whether they had experienced an afterimage that was recognisable as a face (“Yes”, “No”, or “Unsure”). Next, they were asked to generate a visual image of the face of somebody they knew well, with eyes open or closed, for as long as needed to make it as strong and clear as possible (the time spent on this screen was recorded as the imagery duration). Participants then compared their self-generated image with the afterimage, each at its strongest, in terms of overall strength, detail and visual quality, and chose one of five statements. These ranged from the self-generated image being “much stronger, detailed and visual” than the afterimage (relative rating = +2) through “quite similar” (0) to “much weaker, less detailed and visual” (−2). A sixth option allowed them to indicate that they were unsure or found the question impossible to answer; these responses were excluded from analyses. Finally, participants rated how accurate they felt their comparison was (“Very accurate” = 4 to “Very inaccurate” = 1, or “Unsure”). The whole procedure was completed twice. The first run served as practice, and the relative rating from the second run was the main dependent variable, with higher values indicating that self-generated imagery was more vivid relative to the afterimage.

Color Memory Task

Participants performed a color memory task that required them to remember the colors of two simultaneously presented colored patches.

Stimuli

Each colored patch consisted of an 8 × 8 grid of colored squares (64 squares total). Colors were represented in the OKLCH color space, with hue values ranging from 0° to 360°. The colors of individual squares within each patch were drawn from a normal distribution with a mean corresponding to the target color and a standard deviation that could be either 5° or 20° in hue angle. Target colors were selected from four color bins spaced evenly around the 360° color wheel (i.e., at 90° intervals), with random jitter covering the entire bin to ensure the whole color space was sampled. The similarity between the two patches’ mean colors was manipulated across three levels (20°, 45°, or 135° separation in hue angle). The patches were presented to the left and right of a central fixation point.

Trial Procedure

Each trial began with a central fixation circle (2000 ms). The circle briefly disappeared for 100 ms (from 300 to 200 ms before the colored patches appeared) and then reappeared. This was followed by the simultaneous presentation of two colored patches for a variable duration (1500 ms in the main blocks). After a brief memory delay (500 ms), a white circle (cue) appeared either to the left or right of fixation (500 ms), indicating which color patch the participant needed to report. Participants then saw a color wheel and were asked to select the color that best matched the average color of the cued patch by clicking on the appropriate position on the wheel. The color wheel had a random offset on each trial to prevent position-based response strategies. Participants had 5 seconds to respond. If they failed to respond within this time window, they received a “Too late! Try to respond faster next time” message for 2500 ms. After reporting the first color, participants were cued to report the color of the second patch following the same procedure.

Design

The experiment employed a 4 (color bin) × 2 (target position: left, right) × 2 (target standard deviation: 5°, 20°) × 2 (distractor standard deviation: 5°, 20°) × 3 (similarity bin: 20°, 45°, 135°) within-subjects factorial design. Each of the two experimental blocks contained all 96 combinations once, giving 192 trials in total, each with two color reports (one per patch).

Training

Before starting the main experimental trials, participants completed 10 training trials (after which they could choose to complete another 10 training trials or continue to the main task) where stimulus presentation times were initially longer (4000 ms for the colored patches and 1000 ms for the cue) and gradually decreased to match the timing used in the main experiment (1500 ms and 500 ms, respectively). During training, participants received detailed feedback showing both their response and the correct answer after each trial.

Participants’ performance was scored based on the angular deviation between their response and the target color, with higher scores awarded for more accurate responses.

Participants

Forty-five participants took part in the study. Four participants were excluded under the existing memory-quality rules (circular SD of errors above 60 deg. or fewer than 250 main-task report rows).

Results

Imagery and memory scores

The VVIQ scores were between 0 and 63 (M = 40.20 [36.29, 43.98]). Questionnaire scores are missing for 4 sessions without all 16 saved questionnaire responses; a missing questionnaire score does not by itself exclude a session from the memory analyses.

The imagery/afterimage ratings ranged from -2 to 2, with a median of 0 across 44 participants. 19 rated their imagery as weaker than the afterimage, 5 as similar, and 20 as stronger. The rating was missing or unsure for 1 session(s). Only the second run was analyzed; the first was practice.

Memory MAE ranged from 10.46 to 26.87 degrees across 41 participants, with an average of M = 16.56 [15.37, 17.78] degrees (95% confidence interval in brackets). Lower MAE indicates more accurate memory. These scores use the same outlier exclusions and hue-bias correction as the accuracy analyses below.

Color recall accuracy

The data were preprocessed to exclude outliers and correct systematic response biases for different hues.

A three-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested target noise, distractor noise and report order, including all their interactions. The results are summarized below.

Effect Statistics
Target noise F(1, 40) = 167.42, p < .001, \(\eta\)2G = .15
Distractor noise F(1, 40) = 0.09, p = .762, \(\eta\)2G < .01
Report order F(1, 40) = 116.75, p < .001, \(\eta\)2G = .19
Target noise × distractor noise F(1, 40) = 2.45, p = .125, \(\eta\)2G < .01
Target noise × report order F(1, 40) = 0.00, p = .980, \(\eta\)2G < .01
Distractor noise × report order F(1, 40) = 0.28, p = .598, \(\eta\)2G < .01
Target noise × distractor noise × report order F(1, 40) = 6.10, p = .018, \(\eta\)2G < .01

Errors were larger for high-noise targets and for the second report, showing clear effects of target noise and report order. There was no clear overall effect of distractor noise, and none of the two-way interactions reached p < .05. However, the three-way interaction showed that the combined effect of target and distractor noise differed between the first and second reports. The panels in Figure 2 therefore need to be considered separately rather than relying only on effects averaged across reports.

Paired comparisons tested the second minus first report, both overall and within each combination of target and distractor noise. Positive differences mean that the second report was less accurate. The five p-values were adjusted together using Holm’s method.

Comparison N Second minus first (degrees; 95% CI) Test Holm-adjusted p
Target low / distractor low 41 M = 3.56 [2.53, 4.66] t(40.0) = 6.71, p < .001 < .001
Target low / distractor high 41 M = 4.93 [3.87, 5.95] t(40.0) = 9.20, p < .001 < .001
Target high / distractor low 41 M = 4.62 [3.33, 6.02] t(40.0) = 6.90, p < .001 < .001
Target high / distractor high 41 M = 3.89 [2.70, 5.03] t(40.0) = 6.50, p < .001 < .001
All noise conditions 41 M = 4.25 [3.48, 5.06] t(40.0) = 10.81, p < .001 < .001

Across the four noise conditions, the second-report cost was M = 4.25 [3.48, 5.06] degrees. The second report was less accurate in all four noise combinations after adjustment. These comparisons describe the report-order differences; the three-way interaction above tests whether the noise effects themselves change with report order.

How are the two imagery measures related?

We compared VVIQ scores with the second-run imagery/afterimage rating (Figure 3). Higher values on both measures indicate stronger imagery, although one is a questionnaire and the other compares imagery with an afterimage. We used Spearman’s correlation because the afterimage rating has five ordered categories.

Comparison Method N Correlation p
VVIQ – imagery/afterimage Spearman rho 40 0.33 .038

Higher questionnaire scores were associated with stronger imagery relative to the afterimage. This comparison uses 40 participants with both scores, including those excluded only from the memory analyses.

Does imagery ability predict overall color memory performance?

We related each imagery measure to the participant’s memory MAE (Figure 4). A negative correlation would mean that stronger imagery was associated with more accurate memory. VVIQ associations use Pearson’s correlation; imagery/afterimage associations use Spearman’s correlation. Each test uses participants with both of its measures available.

Comparison Method N Correlation p
VVIQ – memory MAE Pearson r 38 0.163 .329
Imagery/afterimage – memory MAE Spearman rho 40 0.069 .672

Neither imagery measure showed a clear association with overall memory accuracy in this sample. These three correlations across the two imagery questions are exploratory and their p-values are unadjusted. Nonsignificant results leave uncertainty about the strength of the relationships.

Does imagery ability predict the effect of noise?

For each person, we calculated how much their average error changed from low to high noise in the target patch. Positive changes mean that noise made memory less accurate. We then checked whether these changes were related to VVIQ scores or imagery/afterimage ratings. Other conditions were weighted equally in these comparisons.

As above, VVIQ associations use Pearson’s correlation and imagery/afterimage associations use Spearman’s correlation. The tables for these last two questions show both the original p-values and p-values adjusted with Holm’s method across their four correlations. These analyses are exploratory.

Comparison Imagery measure N Correlation p Holm-adjusted p
Noise in the target Imagery / afterimage 40 0.206 .202 .606
Noise in the target VVIQ 38 -0.004 .982 .982

Neither imagery measure clearly predicted the effect of noise after adjustment for the four correlations. The estimates and their uncertainty are shown in Figure 5. A nonsignificant result does not establish that imagery has no influence on sensitivity to noise.

Does imagery ability predict the cost of reporting the second item?

We calculated each person’s increase in average error from the first report to the second. Positive values mean that the second report was less accurate. Across participants, this increase was M = 4.35 [3.64, 5.10] degrees (t(40.0) = 11.06, p < .001).

We then asked whether imagery scores predicted this increase. A negative correlation would mean that people with stronger imagery lost less accuracy on their second report.

Imagery measure N Correlation p Holm-adjusted p
Imagery / afterimage 40 0.115 .479 .959
VVIQ 38 -0.309 .059 .238

Neither imagery measure clearly predicted the change from the first report to the second after adjustment for the four correlations. The sample leaves uncertainty about whether people with stronger imagery lose less accuracy on their second report.

The participant comparisons and their correlations are available in imagery_condition_effects.csv and imagery_effect_correlations.csv. All comparisons use the same outlier exclusions as the earlier accuracy analyses.

Correlation matrix across all measures

The matrix brings together the five measures considered above: VVIQ, the imagery/afterimage rating, overall memory MAE, target-noise cost and second-report cost. Each point is a participant. Positive costs mean worse performance with high target noise or on the second report. The matrix repeats the earlier plots and also displays relationships between the memory measures.

Each panel uses participants with both measures available. The full table contains 45 sessions; missing imagery scores do not automatically exclude valid memory data, and memory exclusions do not remove valid imagery scores. The lines are descriptive, including for the ordinal afterimage rating.

Participant scores and pairwise statistics are available in imagery_participant_metrics.csv, imagery_correlations.csv, imagery_condition_effects.csv and imagery_effect_correlations.csv.
